decisions.title: Founder growth is shifting: 7 states growing well above India's 3.3×
decisions.recommendation: New startup recognitions grew fastest in Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Jammu and Kashmir, Punjab, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu, and slowest in Chhattisgarh, Delhi, Karnataka and Kerala. If Rize's buildathon and community-event calendar still follows the 2019 map of where founders were, re-weight it toward where they are arriving now.
evidence: Each state's 2023 share of its own 2019+2023 recognitions tested against the rest of India, Holm-corrected across 23 states; strongest result p < 1e-15. Effect must also exceed 5 percentage points.
decisions.counterEvidence: DPIIT recognition is opt-in, and some state startup policies require it for local benefits — part of a state's growth can be a policy push to register, not new founders. Check against company-incorporation counts (MCA) for the same states before moving budget.
decisions.source: DPIIT recognitions by state, PIB Feb 2024

decisions.title: Gujarat: a fast-growing founder base that almost never reaches YC
decisions.recommendation: Gujarat is one of India's fastest-growing startup states, but it sends far fewer companies to YC per recognised startup than the rest of the country. That's where Rize for YC adds the most: run targeted application clinics and founder office hours there, rather than in Bengaluru, where founders already find their way to YC.

impactRange.label: Gujarat: YC admits per 1,000 recognised startups

evidence: Gujarat: 1 YC admit(s) from 8,619 recognised startups, 2019–2023.
YC admits ÷ DPIIT recognitions by state, Holm-corrected across 32 states; strongest p = 2.62e-4. Rate ratio must be at least 1.5× either way.
2 of 174 Indian YC companies in the window had no mappable state and are excluded.
decisions.counterEvidence: This is a ratio of two different populations, not a tracked conversion: a YC company need not be DPIIT-recognised, and founders often relocate to Bengaluru before applying, so YC lists them there. Sector mix matters too — a state heavy in services or trading startups will send fewer to YC regardless of outreach.
decisions.source: yc-oss YC directory + DPIIT recognitions, PIB Feb 2024

decisions.title: Karnataka supplies most of India's YC companies
decisions.recommendation: Measure Rize for YC on admits from outside Karnataka. Admits from there would mostly happen anyway; admits from elsewhere are the ones Rize can credibly claim.

impactRange.label: Karnataka's share of Indian YC admits, 2019–2023

evidence: Karnataka: 98 admits from 10,874 recognitions (9.01 per 1,000 vs 0.79 elsewhere).
decisions.counterEvidence: Some of this is relocation: founders from other states move to Bengaluru and list it as their location. The real gap between states is probably smaller than the location field suggests.
decisions.source: yc-oss YC directory + DPIIT recognitions, PIB Feb 2024

decisions.title: India's share of YC fell from 7.6% to 1.1%
decisions.recommendation: Getting Indian founders into YC is much harder now than in 2019–2022. Set Rize for YC's targets against this smaller base, and put the effort into application quality rather than application volume.
evidence: Two-proportion test: p < 1e-15. The 2022/2023 split was chosen after looking at the yearly series, so treat this p-value as descriptive.
decisions.counterEvidence: YC's location field reflects where companies say they are now. Indian-founded companies that moved their headquarters to the US are counted as US companies, which may understate India's share, especially in recent batches.

decisions.title: Gujarat, Kerala, Chhattisgarh and Jammu and Kashmir: fewer startups with a woman director
decisions.recommendation: About 50% of India's recognised startups have at least one woman director or partner, but Gujarat, Kerala, Chhattisgarh and Jammu and Kashmir sit well below that. If Rize runs women-founder or D2C+ programmes, these states are the gap to close.

impactRange.label: Gujarat: share with a woman director/partner

evidence: Jammu and Kashmir: 228 of 624 recognitions in 2019–2023 (36.5%).
Holm-corrected across 32 states; strongest p < 1e-15. Gap must exceed 5 percentage points.
decisions.counterEvidence: "At least one woman director or partner" is not the same as woman-founded or woman-led: family-run companies often add a woman director for compliance. The two tables also come from releases two years apart, so a few recognitions may have been revised in between.
decisions.source: DPIIT women-director table, PIB Feb 2026 + recognitions, PIB Feb 2024

withheld.title: Closure rates by state: not called
reason: Gujarat's closure rate (3.0% vs 4.7% elsewhere) is statistically significant, but Gujarat is also one of the fastest-growing states. A younger set of startups has had less time to close, so state-level totals can't separate "healthier ecosystem" from "younger startups".
Karnataka (5.6% vs 4.4%) is statistically significant but under the 1.5× size bar, so it isn't worth acting on.
Tamil Nadu (3.7% vs 4.6%) is statistically significant but under the 1.5× size bar, so it isn't worth acting on.
withheld.whatWouldSettleIt: Closures broken down by recognition year (the cohort) for each state. That would let the engine compare startups of the same age.

withheld.title: Survival of recent Indian YC companies: too new to call
reason: 2024 (n=7), 2025 (n=3), 2026 (n=6): fewer than 3 years old. "Still active" doesn't mean much yet, and every one of these cohorts is also below the minimum sample of 30.
withheld.whatWouldSettleIt: Time. These cohorts become readable once they are 3 years old.
